column2: Act Eleven
The Engagement
Engagement

Nono would always be the fierce little red-haired witch driving a Ferrari, ruthless and full of mischief. Marriage would still be a distant future for her; she had yet to learn to cook, stubbornly preferred ice cream close to the color of her hair, and raced with him down dark mountain roads...
But things would change. Everyone would leave, and he would be left where he was.
The CC1000 branch express raced across the fields of early autumn. Beneath a blue sky washed clean, the vegetation shifted from deep green to gold to reddish brown, changing like a rainbow.
Andrew Gattuso, head of the investigation team, admired the magnificent view with a calm, dignified expression, though emotions surged within him.

He was the Gattuso family's chief legal counsel, a Yale Law School graduate who had attended the same university as several American presidents. He was also a hybrid. Unfortunately, his talent for Yanling was limited, so he had spent the first half of his life in charge of the consortium's legal affairs, never directly involving himself in the family's largest investment, the College. But he understood its importance. It consumed money, yet it mattered more than all the family's profitable institutions. The College brought together the finest hybrids in every field. A hybrid who had never set foot there, never sat down to speak with its tenured professors and won their approval, was second-rate in the eyes of other hybrids, no matter how successful he was in the world of ordinary humans.

Today he had finally won his chance. He was not making a pilgrimage to the College; he had received the Board of Trustees' highest authorization to impeach the tyrannical principal who had been running amok there.
He would display his talent before the greatest hybrid elites. His powers of analysis, his logical mind, his profoundly moving eloquence: all seemed to have been prepared for this day.
Andrew Gattuso: that name would go down in history as a legal genius among hybrids! And the code of law he wielded was the sacred Abraham Bloodline Covenant!
“We'll arrive at the terminal in five minutes. The train has begun to slow.” The young secretary entered the VIP car and bowed slightly.

Andrew nodded, reasonably pleased with the secretary's efficiency. The young man, Parsi, had been assigned to the delegation by Mr. Frost Gattuso, who considered him worth cultivating. Andrew thought that although he was nowhere near as spirited as Andrew himself had been at his age, he was at least obedient. Andrew did not much like Parsi's taste in hairstyles, however. The secretary always combed his beautiful blond hair into long bangs that covered his eyes, and Andrew could never see them clearly. Andrew thought it very bad not to look one's superior honestly in the eye.
“Has the College been informed of our arrival time?” Andrew adjusted his collar.
“Yes. They said they would meet us at the station.”

“Good. You're very thorough.” Andrew generously offered the young man encouragement. “Are they still calm?” He imagined the old fellow who had occupied the principal's seat for nearly a century hearing that the Board was openly investigating him. Surely it would feel like a thunderbolt from the blue.
“I couldn't tell over the phone.”

Andrew remembered something and put on a stern face. “Remember, we're here on behalf of the Board. Everything must be strictly official. Don't have too much contact with them outside work, or they may influence you.”

“Understood!” Parsi hesitated. “But impeaching the principal requires more than the Board. All the tenured professors have to vote. Until Principal Anjou has been found negligent, could we take a gentler approach?”
“Gentler?” Andrew said coldly. “We already have more than enough evidence regarding Anjou, and that student Chu Zihang!”

“One is president of the Lionheart Society, a student leader, and the other is the principal. If we handle this badly,” Parsi said softly, “I'm afraid the students' emotions could get out of control.”

Andrew sneered, not bothering to comment on Parsi's childish worry. What if the students lost control? Would they defy the Board? Riot? They should not forget that the Board—or rather, the Secret Party's council of elders—was itself the most powerful institution of force!

“Arrange my schedule. I want to visit every department head and every tenured professor. If Anjou cooperates with our investigation, I can have a friendly conversation with him. If he chooses to resist, there's no need for me to see him!” Andrew's tone was uncompromising.
“Understood.”

At the sound of the whistle as the train entered the station, Andrew sprang to his feet, face stern and chest out, like a warrior going to battle. “Cassell College was founded as a military academy against the dragons. Now it is time to put it back on the right track!”
“Welcome, welcome! A warm welcome!”
“Welcome to the Board's investigation team! We look forward to your guidance.”
“Professor Andrew, you've had a long journey!”
Andrew had barely stepped out of the car when cheers like these washed over him.

What was going on? Something seemed wrong. Had they stopped at the wrong station? Was he hearing things? Shouldn't the principal be waiting nervously beside a black sedan, looking grief-stricken as he awaited this imperial envoy? Andrew had prepared himself. If Anjou tried to curry favor before the investigation by inviting him to afternoon tea, he would refuse on principle: “I'm here to work, not drink tea.”

But why was there a parade float? With banners streaming and colorful flags waving... And what were all those boys and girls on the platform doing with bouquets in their hands? Good Lord! A middle-aged fellow appeared beside him, wearing a bright-red Hawaiian shirt and plastic-framed sunglasses, and rushed up to embrace him!
He must have entered some wrong dimension and seen a bizarre scene. Surely if he stepped back into the train, closed the door, and opened it again, everything would return to normal!

Andrew had no time to close the door. The scruffy man swept him into a deep embrace and pounded his back as though trying to stop him coughing. The heavy smell of alcohol made Andrew dizzy. A pretty girl appeared beside them and slipped a Hawaiian-style lei around his neck. Surrounded by the crowd, he stumbled onto the float decked in red and green.
“Is this... a kidnapping?” Andrew was utterly bewildered.
Parsi hurried after him and leaned close to his ear. “This should be the procession the College sent to welcome you. This gentleman is probably... the vice principal!”
“The vice principal?” Andrew's mind went blank. He had read the College's documents. Did the place actually have a vice principal? He had never seen a vice principal's signature on any document.
“He's the Night Watcher,” Parsi whispered. “Vice principal is an honorary title. He doesn't handle any specific duties.”

The words “Night Watcher” startled Andrew. He looked the figure up and down, somewhere between a scruffy middle-aged man and a scruffy old grandfather, and could not possibly connect him with the person in the photograph. The College's number two, the Night Watcher, was an important figure hidden in the shadows. Andrew had researched him before coming and even obtained a photograph, though it had been taken in Bolivia in 1934... But however swiftly the years passed, surely he could not have changed this much? Where was the sculpted, handsome face? The high Greek nose? The long, slender curls somewhere between a rake's and a young rocker's? The eyes, both seductive and innocent, that could enchant women from young wives to grandmothers?
Time had made the old fellow into a complete tragedy!

The vice principal apparently had no idea what Andrew was thinking. He leaned in, nodding repeatedly and radiating enthusiasm. “We've been waiting for you! I've thought for ages it was time someone dealt with him. He lives as long as a tortoise! He's kept me vice principal all these years!”

Hundreds of students held bouquets aloft around the float as it rolled slowly along. The crowd roared, balloons and ribbons flew through the air, and the faint sound of champagne corks popping could be heard. They all seemed delighted by the investigation team's visit, ready to turn it into a grand College festival.

The vice principal put an arm around Andrew's shoulders, his face full of pride. “The students are in good spirits, aren't they?” He gave a vigorous thumbs-up. “I knew the investigation team would be pleased!”
Without giving Andrew a chance to answer, he raised an arm high. “Hello, students! Thank you for all your hard work!”
The students responded loudly, “Hello, sir! You're the one who works hardest...”
Andrew had no idea this “wrong welcome” was only the beginning of a succession of mistakes... Starting with the banquet, the mistake plunged into an utterly irreversible abyss!

Principal Hilbert Jean Anjou did not appear at all, much less invite him to afternoon tea. Reportedly, he was suffering from a severe throat infection. The hospitable vice principal took over all reception duties on behalf of the College's management. “You've come to investigate him, so he's upset!” he told Andrew privately.
“Never mind him. It wasn't easy getting here, so you should eat well. No need to stand on ceremony; just call me Old Mei.” The vice principal kept Andrew's arm tightly linked in his all the way.

The banquet was authentic Chinese cuisine. The appetizer was Indian aster and shredded tofu salad, the main course roast duck from an open oven, and the soup hot-and-sour soup with dough pieces... The sommelier filled everyone's glass with a potent spirit called erguotou. Before Andrew could object, the vice principal embraced him and steered him to his seat. “If you won't drink with me, I won't help you deal with Anjou! You've got to give me face!” His heartfelt loyalty to the Board could have been witnessed by sun and moon. Accustomed to red wine, Andrew had never imagined such a clear, pure liquid could burn so fiercely. When the vice principal raised his glass, said “Let's knock one back,” and drained it, Andrew assumed it was some kind of custom and drained his too.

“You can really hold your liquor!” the vice principal exclaimed. What followed was the opening of one bottle of erguotou after another, with the exuberance of champagne being opened at a grand wedding.

Andrew could hardly refuse such kindness. The vice principal had not only declared his loyalty to the Board, but had brought in department heads and tenured professors to join them. These were precisely the people Andrew had planned to divide and win over before coming. So he had no choice but to summon his courage and imitate the vice principal, carrying a little glass liquor pot around the round table and drinking with each of them in turn.

“Mr. Vice Principal, aren't you... French?” Andrew, swaying on his feet, finally realized this reception was exactly like a Chinese township welcoming officials on an inspection visit. He had once represented the consortium on a trip to China to study its investment climate.

“Yes, born and raised in Paris.” The vice principal widened his eyes. “You think I have a bit of Chinese style, don't you? During World War II I helped Chennault set up the Flying Tigers in China and lived there for more than ten years. I can even sing Chinese folk songs...”

In high spirits, the vice principal threw back his head and sang several songs. The only words Andrew could remember were: “When friends come, there's good wine; if jackals come, hunting rifles will welcome them...”

The next day, Andrew was still hungover when the enthusiastic vice principal woke him by phone to visit one of the College's special programs: radio calisthenics. Supposedly the vice principal had learned this advanced practice while fighting the Japanese in China, and the College's Chinese-language instruction over the past decade had also been proposed by him.

The third day's program was a visit to the College's award ceremony for “Three-Good Students,” naturally another Chinese educational tradition. It was solemn yet lively, but only at the end did Andrew discover that this year's recipient was Chu Zihang, the subject of his investigation...

The fourth day's program was an examination for the female students' deep-water certification. Andrew had no choice but to accept the vice principal's kindly arrangements, change into swim trunks, and sit with him on lounge chairs beside the pool, drinking erguotou over ice while watching girls in white bikinis dive gracefully into the water, their lotus-root-like arms rising and falling as they broke the clear surface.
“Nice view, isn't it?” The vice principal beamed and lowered his voice. “I've always thought the girls at our College have great figures!”

Over those days Andrew's entire worldview came close to collapse. He did not know what sort of people the family's years of investment had been supporting at the College. Weren't they supposed to be landmark figures in science, towering authorities in the occult, Executive Department commissioners with wills of steel? This was supposed to be a sacred hall of learning admired by all hybrids, yet besides its flamboyant, domineering principal, it had an even more flamboyant and sleazy vice principal!
On the evening of the fourth day, filled with grief and indignation, he phoned Frost Gattuso in Rome.
Late at night, a light was still burning in the Night Watcher's little attic in the bell tower.

“A record full of misconduct! Absolutely full of it!” The vice principal slapped the papers in his hand, distraught. “My old friend, no wonder they're investigating you. Your actions during your time as principal can only be described as lawless, all right?”

“As vice principal, you collect your salary every month without fail, but a sleazy fellow who just hides in the attic drinking and reading adult magazines isn't qualified to say that, is he?” Anjou's brows drooped. He looked a little dispirited. The papers in the Night Watcher's hands were the Board's formal impeachment documents, clearly organized and supported by solid evidence. This investigation team seemed serious. After the fourth day, Andrew had abruptly become tough, coldly refusing all the vice principal's planned activities and then releasing the documents publicly.
“The rest is easy enough. I already explained things like ‘giving extra attention to young, pretty girls’ for you... But this business with Chu Zihang...” The Night Watcher scratched his head.
“Hey, how did you explain it?” Anjou felt inexplicably nervous.

“I said you're old and have little pleasure left in life, so spending time with young girls is good for your cardiovascular health and does no harm. And you're very attentive to little boys like Lu Mingfei too, so there's no sign you have improper intentions...”
“Hey! Are you the one the Board sent to smear me?”

“Let's set that aside and talk about Chu Zihang. He's your weak point now, and you've decided to protect him. Don't underestimate this team. Andrew may be useless, but Frost must be directing him from behind the scenes. After a brief period of confusion, they've regrouped and launched an attack, concentrating all their fire on Chu Zihang in front of every department head. The department heads are the College's core strength. If they decide you aren't fit to remain principal, that's when you'll really be thrown out. They won't care if your private life is disreputable...”
“Hey! My private life isn't disreputable!” Anjou protested.

“I said those were small matters! Set them aside!” The vice principal sounded very broad-minded. “But the department heads will care that you brought a dangerous bloodline onto campus. That's your fatal weakness. They've already decided to hold a hearing. In name it's a hearing, but in reality it's a court to try you, with Chu Zihang standing trial in your place. The two of you are tied together now. If he goes down, you go down with him. All the tenured professors are the jury, and King Solomon, the leader of the professors, is the judge.”
“Can we assign Chu Zihang a lawyer?”
“You have me! Your reliable old friend! I'll represent the College's management and tear into the investigation team. Just watch my magnificent performance!”
Anjou glanced at him. “You look suspicious...”

“In any case, I'm the only lawyer you can send out now... or enforcer. Want some professional advice from your lawyer?” The vice principal crossed his legs like a seasoned shyster and blew clouds of smoke.
“All right.” Anjou shrugged. “What should we do to prepare to win this trial?”
The vice principal held his hand like a blade and chopped downward. “Naturally, destroy the evidence!”
“You have absolutely no sense of morality... but I like it. All right, let's talk about how to destroy the evidence.” Anjou nodded.
“We have someone even more professional at destroying evidence!” The vice principal clapped and called, “Come in!”

The door opened. Anjou drew a sharp breath, staring in shock at the face wearing a thoroughly loserish grin. “Fingel? Haven't you graduated? Weren't you sent away as an Executive Department commissioner? Why are you here?”
“At your service, Principal!” Fingel bobbed and bowed.
“The College's finest news expert, though his grades are a little poor.” The vice principal clapped Fingel's shoulder vigorously. “He already has a preliminary plan for winning this trial.”
“He's a student! Involving him will let him learn too much that he shouldn't know!” Anjou's tone was icy. “Those who know too much aren't usually the longest-lived among us!”

“You have to trust our young people!” The vice principal put an arm around Fingel's neck. “Just as you chose Lu Mingfei, Fingel is the one I chose. Don't look so surprised. Think of the name of the campus forum.”
Anjou remembered. The forum was called... the Night Watcher forum.

Everything was easy to explain now. The name was not merely an expression of the students' respect for the vice principal. He was the mastermind behind it. Between drinking and reading magazines of beautiful women in his attic, he had also spared no effort cultivating his own power among the students. He controlled the News Department, that shameless band of paparazzi who dared post Anjou's official travel bills and photographs of department heads' first girlfriends online. In the end, almost nobody on campus dared offend the News Department lightly.
Anjou restrained the urge to throw tables and chairs at the pair. “All right, Fingel. Can you keep a secret? What are your conditions?”
“Please let me graduate.” Fingel stood at attention.
“You're... from the class of 2001, aren't you? You still haven't graduated?” Anjou was startled. In a corner he had never paid attention to, a loser like this was still hanging on.
“Principal, you've touched a sore spot...”

“All right. It's a deal. If Chu Zihang can remain enrolled after the hearing, you'll graduate at the end of the academic year.” Anjou sighed. “How could this happen? You were an A-rank we placed great hopes in!”
“I'm G-rank now...” For once, even Fingel looked embarrassed.
“There's... a rank that low?” Anjou was shocked again.
“They created it for me... because I got demoted again.”
Anjou shook his head. “All right. I suppose the vice principal has told you everything. I know we have plenty of evidence we can't conceal. Tell me your plan.”

Fingel opened a folder, his voice low and manner professional. “Chu Zihang, third-year, A-rank student, a key cultivation target for the College. He has thirteen missions behind him. Contrary to his mild outward appearance, his methods are forceful and reckless. Take this mission in China: his nearly uncontrolled actions sent fifty-three people to the hospital. The fact that nobody died was only luck. The records show thirteen missions and thirteen disciplinary citations. If Professor Schneider of the Executive Department weren't his adviser, he'd have been expelled long ago. Add his golden eyes that can't be extinguished and his dangerous Yanling, and his continued enrollment really is a failure of our management.”
“It's that serious?” Anjou found his head aching too.
“His misdeeds are notorious, his crimes unforgivable!” Fingel declared firmly.
“Can we still clean up his image?”
“About as difficult as washing a lump of coal white.”
Anjou pressed a hand to his forehead.

“Worst of all, because his style is so outrageous, many of the troubles he caused were reported by local news media. Though the newspapers and TV programs didn't name him, tens of millions of papers around the world indirectly documented his ‘outstanding operational effectiveness.’ The investigation team will present all of them to the jury as evidence,” Fingel said.
“Could you give me some good news?” Anjou sighed. He was beginning to suspect that as an educator he really was as unqualified as the Board claimed.

“That's why we need Fingel. Know who spreads your little secrets all over the world?” the vice principal said. “Not WikiLeaks. The paparazzi. They're the most dedicated journalists in the world, with an unrivaled nose for gossip. They're skeptics who doubt everything, get in everywhere, and possess all the virtues of journalists. They'll search a female star's trash for the packaging from her new underwear to deduce whether she's had plastic surgery.” The vice principal raised an eyebrow and spoke with pride. “But the people best at finding secrets are also the best at hiding them!”
“We specialize in washing coal white!” Fingel puffed out his chest.
“All right, go on.” Anjou waved helplessly.

“Norma and Chu Zihang himself are also evidence. Norma keeps all the College's data, but we can't alter it anymore. The Board must already have examined all Norma's records and archived them,” Fingel said. “More troublesome than Norma is Chu Zihang.”
“Oh?” Anjou frowned.

“His blood sample,” the vice principal said slowly. “Blood amplification was a technique your Lionheart Society originally invented. You should remember its side effects. It's forbidden because every time the user amplifies their blood, their genes are altered to become more dragonlike. Once the Board gets his blood sample, it'll be irrefutable proof.”
“How do we deal with that evidence?”
“Kill the witness! Destroy the body! Let's rush to the ward now! Slaughter Chu Zihang! Burn him to ashes!” Fingel's eyes flashed viciously.
Anjou could not be bothered with this clown. He covered his face and thought for a moment. “Leave it to me. I have a way.”

“Then there's only one thing left: witnesses. Some students have seen Chu Zihang on the verge of losing control, and there are plenty of rumors about him. The good news is that the Lionheart Society is one of the largest student organizations, and they'll undoubtedly stand behind their president. The bad news is that the Student Council is his sworn enemy, and Caesar will undoubtedly undermine him,” Fingel said.
“That's something we can't resolve.” Anjou pondered for a long time. “Then what are our chances at the hearing, my dear lawyer?”

“Fifty-fifty. If Frost weren't directing things, I could absolutely drink that good-for-nothing Andrew under the table... I mean, beat him in debate. But with Frost behind the scenes, I only have an even chance.” The vice principal sighed.

“We must win the tenured professors' support, and quickly. This is a critical moment. They have another purpose in launching this impeachment against me.” Anjou drained the strong liquor in his glass. “Hybrids all over the world know a dragon of exalted status has awakened, perhaps even a Dragon King. The Board families, and those under Henkel, are searching for him all over the world. Killing a Dragon King has been proven possible. They all want to kill that dragon before anyone else and claim his remains. And the Board has tied us up here with this strange lawsuit.”
“The hearing will be held in three days, in the great conference hall of Valhalla,” Fingel said.

“Then the battle between us and the Board has to begin tonight. They'll be staying up late preparing material to bring us down too.” The vice principal tossed Fingel a ring of keys. “From now on you have authority to use the Central Control Room. Take your team in. Suspend the Executive Department's operations around the world! We'll take on the Board first!”

At midnight, Parsi, secretary to the investigation team, sat in darkness and breathed deeply. Once he was certain he had reached his optimal state, he opened the laptop before him. Its faint light illuminated his face, and his nonprescription lenses reflected lines of rapidly flashing dark-green characters.

From a hard aluminum-alloy combination case, he took a black envelope and tipped out a silvery metal card. It was solid metal, with no exposed chip and no magnetic stripe. Parsi ran his fingers across its surface, feeling a faint pattern.

A special card slot was already connected to the laptop's USB port. Parsi slipped the metal card in. A few seconds later, the interface refreshed. It was extremely crude: simple blocks of color and rough-edged lettering, without any graphic decoration, pure old-fashioned engineering style. Cassell College's network backend was rough not because its level was low, but because so few people used it.
Those who could use this page did not care about aesthetics. What mattered to them was access.
The highest access.
“Mr. Gattuso, I've connected to Norma.” Parsi called and put the phone on speaker. “Awaiting your orders.”

“Good.” Frost Gattuso's voice was severe. “You now have Norma's highest authorization, granted by the white card. You can access every corner of Norma, but no one else can see a record of your visits. Use that power carefully. I shouldn't have entrusted the white card to you, but they were shameless enough to cut off the network, so I had no choice but to have you log in from inside the College.”
“Yes, sir.”

That afternoon, Frost had been unable to connect to Norma from Europe as usual. More precisely, internet communication between the entire North American continent and Europe had been disrupted. Reuters reported that a transatlantic undersea cable might have been bitten through by a sperm whale. Only Frost understood the full sequence: a few hours before the cable was cut, the investigation team had announced its major decision to hold a hearing. And when the cable broke, the distinguished tug Moniach, which had carried out Operation Bronze at the Three Gorges, had happened to pass through those waters... Frost had not expected the two old men to be this shameless.

“Some of the data in Norma's core storage has always been impossible for us to decrypt. We back it up every month. They must be hiding something in those encrypted files. Once Anjou is removed as principal, we'll take over Norma. They'll certainly delete the data first. They have the principal's and vice principal's two black cards. But you hold the white card and have supreme authorization! First set the data to read-only, then begin the backup.”
“Understood.” Parsi's fingers danced over the keyboard like a peerless dancer on a red-hot iron plate.
Meanwhile, in the Central Control Room.
Every entrance had been locked. Unauthorized people, even members of the Executive Department, were forbidden to approach. A top-secret team had moved in before midnight.
Cassell College, News Department.

Alchemical cipher machines printed at high speed with a crisp clatter. Vast quantities of news photographs were downloaded by way of the College's secret server cluster in Asia; videos appeared as 3D projections in the center of the hall... If the data streams were represented as dark-green strings of numbers like those in The Matrix, digital torrents from around the world would now be surging toward the man in the center, overwhelming as ten thousand rivers flowing to the sea.

That man had his feet on an expensive walnut desk and drank Coke by the mouthful, tossing aside each document after reading it. Printed pages covered the floor, another mountain of files stood on the desk, and there were enough empty Coke cans to line up like dominoes.

“This is a post on the Tianya forum titled ‘Holy crap! What are superpowers? This is what superpowers are!’ The author must have seen Chu Zihang unleash Sovereign Flame. It has 76,239 views and 8,734 replies, and made the front page!” The head of the News Department's First Section hurried over and handed him a printout of the page.

“Do you have to bother me with something this small? Have the guys flood it with another two thousand replies, and get an administrator to change the posting time. The replies should say things like ‘Don't be stupid, are you crazy?’ or ‘Ha ha ha, that's my cousin who's a magician. He fooled you!’ or ‘The original poster always writes alarmist stuff like this. Stop chasing rumors and be realistic.’ You know what to do! Go!” Fingel waved a hand grandly.
“Our contact at the Associated Press says he'll take that report off their website for a thousand dollars!” someone called.
“Give him two thousand and tell him to clear the comments too!” Fingel waved again.
“The chief is amazing!” marveled the junior massaging his shoulders from behind.
“Of course. You want to know what efficiency is? This is efficiency!” Fingel grunted.
“Once you graduate this time, you can pay us back, right?” the junior asked cautiously.
“No problem!” Fingel gave him a sidelong glance. “The principal said if I do this well, he'll not only let me graduate, he'll clear my credit-card balance and help pay off my debts!”

The junior was almost moved to tears. “Then we'll make absolutely sure our boss graduates! From this moment on, Chu Zihang is a flawless perfect man in our eyes! Anyone who dares tell us he's bad will have us to answer to!”

“We'll make them answer for it!” The paparazzi, busy at their laptops, all raised their hands and shouted together. They were Fingel's juniors and underlings, but also his creditors. Soon after joining the News Department, while they were still finding their feet, Fingel had worn them down and borrowed varying amounts of money. Their loyalty to the department all these years... was also a way to keep a close eye on the man who owed them money.
“Boss, there's something here that's hard to deal with... It's a video,” someone said.
“Project it onto the central screen!” Fingel tossed an empty Coke can.

It appeared to be black-and-white footage from a surveillance camera, thick with static and extremely poor in quality. It looked up at an old building at night, black windows packed together and searchlight beams rising from below. The time flashed in the lower right corner. The silence made one's skin crawl.
“Why does it look like a horror movie?” someone whispered.

Suddenly a dark figure appeared on screen, leaping out after smashing through a window. Another figure followed, a sword in one hand and a nylon fire hose in the other. The two fell together. The second figure kicked hard against the wall and, finding a point of leverage in that instant, hurled his long sword. It pierced the first man's chest. His heart must have ruptured, for blood sprayed from the wound in his back, splashing a wet red streak across the facade as if from a giant spray can. Finally the blood-soaked figure slammed into the ground. The second man landed safely holding the hose, looked coldly around, walked over to the body and pulled out his sword. He wiped the blood on his shoe sole and was about to leave when he noticed the camera, approached, and kicked it. Only static remained on screen.
They could not see his face, but his blazing eyes left the paparazzi in no doubt about his identity.
“So cold... so vicious!” someone said in a trembling voice.
“What is this?” Fingel asked.

“Front-page headline in The New York Times, April 2009: the baby-cutting case solved, the killer dead. It was actually one of Chu Zihang's missions. A hybrid had been operating at a hospital in Brooklyn, New York, cutting unborn babies from pregnant women, probably for some alchemical experiment of a black-magic nature. Chu Zihang disguised himself as a pregnant woman and went undercover at the hospital. He finally found the target and killed him by throwing his sword. This is the hospital's surveillance footage. Chu Zihang was disciplined because the scene was too horrifying: half the hospital wall was blood-red. It triggered extensive media coverage and threatened the College's secrecy,” someone said.
“If that video is used as evidence, it'll be very bad for us,” someone sighed.
“An affront to public morals!” Fingel sighed.
“Boss, wrong phrase. It's cruel and violent,” the head of the Second Section corrected.
“Oh, I mean Chu Zihang actually stayed in the hospital with pregnant women for eleven days, sneaking looks at the naked expectant mothers...”

The juniors exchanged glances and fell silent for a long time. “Boss... there's a problem. Time is short, and this guy's record is practically a story high! And besides that, there's something even more troublesome. He blew up a building during an operation in Cape Town! It would have been one thing if it had been an ordinary building, but he blew up the Cape Town baseball center. That night the local professional teams were playing the final, and tens of thousands of spectators waiting outside to get in saw the whole thing...”
“If we explain it as a mass hallucination involving tens of thousands... probably no one would believe it, would they?” Fingel mused.

“In April 2010, Stockholm's ‘Night Wanderer’ serial murder case. The killer was contaminated by dragon blood from an unknown source and turned into a death servitor. Chu Zihang encountered him before dawn and hanged him with a noose in front of City Hall, a landmark all tourists pass... The scene had a very religious feel. Locals believed it was God's punishment for the killer, and the Pope even came in person to hold a grand Mass for the victims!”

“December 2009, Chicago, the Hancock Building. The west wall from the thirteenth to fifteenth floors was instantly destroyed by a shock wave because Chu Zihang used a weapon the Equipment Department claimed was still ‘in the experimental stage’: ‘Dragon's Breath of Light and Dust.’ It was originally considered reliable, portable individual combat equipment, like a handgun... but for some reason the final effect was a high-intensity shock wave. The weapon was melted down and reforged after the operation... and hasn't been put back into service to this day.”
“He's really gone too far!” Fingel thrust all ten fingers into his disheveled hair.

The mood was heavy. Though they considered themselves experts at washing coal white, even the paparazzi were disheartened by this mountain of incidents. Once something had reached the news media, it was hard to contain. Public media had too much influence; they could neither recall and destroy millions of newspapers nor brainwash the entire world.

“Let's just deny it to the bitter end! What do the perverted killer who was hanged or the collapsed Cape Town baseball stadium have to do with Chu Zihang?” One paparazzo stood and slammed the table, with the ruthlessness of a man going all in. “Chu Zihang just happened to be there on a mission. Coincidence! It was all coincidence! The CIA has done this before. They send agents to a small Latin American country to turn the military against its government, then come back and say the coup had nothing to do with them. They just happened to be traveling there, and even brought back cigars.”
